title: Lumenary EE
subtitle: Electrical engineering from a first circuit to the chips, power grids and radios of 2026: circuits, electronics, digital design, signals and control, embedded systems, communications, power and energy.
description: Lumenary EE is the third subject of Lumenary Scientia, free and open source like Lumenary Math and Lumenary CS. It starts with no experience at all — what a current is and why a bulb lights — and climbs through circuit analysis, analog and digital electronics, signals and control, embedded systems, electromagnetics and communications, and power and energy, to the engineering behind today's chips, AI data centres and energy transition.

Every lesson teaches with ideas first and calculation second. Calculations and simulations are in Python with NumPy, and every block with a **Run in browser** button runs there, with nothing to install. Hardware descriptions in Verilog and circuit netlists for SPICE are run by Lumenary's own checks with Icarus Verilog and ngspice. A lesson says *Code tested* only when all of its code passed. Lumenary EE shares ground with [Lumenary CS](/en/cs/) (how a processor is built from gates) and [Lumenary Robotics](/en/robotics/) (control, sensors and motors), and links to them where they meet.

Electricity can hurt you. Lessons that involve building anything say what is safe — small batteries and current-limited bench supplies — and what is not: never experiment with mains electricity, and leave mains wiring to qualified electricians.

Every lesson was drafted with AI assistance and is awaiting review by a human electrical engineer. The text, exercises and code are original and licensed CC BY-SA 4.0 (code Apache-2.0). Where a manufacturer, laboratory or standards body has published the primary source — a datasheet, an application note, a paper, a standard — the lesson links to it rather than retelling it.

levels.title: Electricity from scratch
levels.summary: No experience needed, from about age 11. What charge, current and voltage are, why a circuit needs a loop, Ohm's law, power and energy, how magnets make motors turn, and how to build and measure circuits safely.

levels.title: Circuit analysis
levels.summary: The engineer's tools for any circuit: Kirchhoff's laws, nodal and mesh analysis, Thévenin and Norton equivalents, capacitors and inductors over time, resonance, AC phasors and impedance, and frequency response.

levels.title: Analog electronics
levels.summary: From the physics of semiconductors to working circuits: diodes, bipolar and MOS transistors, amplifiers, operational amplifiers, feedback and oscillation, power supplies and noise.

levels.title: Digital design
levels.summary: How bits become hardware: Boolean algebra and CMOS gates, combinational and sequential logic, finite-state machines, Verilog and FPGAs, timing, and the design of a simple processor.

levels.title: Signals, systems and control
levels.summary: The mathematics engineers use to describe and shape signals: linear time-invariant systems and convolution, Fourier analysis, sampling and the FFT, digital filters, the Laplace transform and stability, and feedback control.

levels.title: Embedded systems
levels.summary: Computers inside things: microcontrollers and embedded C, sensors and data conversion, the buses chips use to talk to each other, real-time and low-power design, and printed circuit boards.

levels.title: Electromagnetics and communications
levels.summary: How energy and information travel: Maxwell's equations and electromagnetic waves, transmission lines and matching, antennas and radio links, modulation, information theory and error-correcting codes, and the wireless systems of 2026.

levels.title: Power and energy
levels.summary: The engineering of electric power: three-phase systems, transformers and electric machines, power electronics, how the grid stays stable, and the renewable sources, storage and electric vehicles of the energy transition.

levels.title: The frontier of electrical engineering
levels.summary: Where the field is moving in 2026, with links to the primary sources: transistors at the 2-nanometre scale, how chips are designed, hardware for AI, powering data centres, photonics, and the engineering of quantum computers.
